lines: A shop's data catalog last scanned everything on a Sunday.

By Wednesday, one table's been dropped, a new one's shown up, and a column's been renamed somewhere else entirely. Thursday rolls around, somebody goes looking, and finds the old table — still sitting there, confidently marked as certified.
So, to actually catch that within seconds instead of days — what does it take?
Does scanning more often close that gap on its own? Does switching over to event-based updates do it? Or does it genuinely take both? Think that through before I go on.
answer: Scanning more often only ever shrinks that gap — it never actually closes it. However often that scan runs, there's always some window afterward where a change has happened and nobody's caught it yet.
An event-based update is a different animal entirely. It fires the instant something changes, so there's no window sitting there waiting to be caught at all.

lines: So what is a catalog actually holding onto, underneath all of this?

A table. A column. A person. A tag. Each one of those is a single point sitting in a graph. And connections between them — someone owns this, this comes from that — those are named links drawn between two of those points.
All of that, held together in one place, and searchable.
There are really only two ways any of that information actually gets in.
One: something sweeps through a source system on a fixed schedule and reports back what it found. That's stale for exactly as long as its own schedule says, every single time, no exceptions.
Two: the source system itself fires off an update the instant something actually changes. That one's never stale at all — there's no schedule for it to wait on in the first place.
Put yourself in the shoes of somebody actually using this thing day to day. What are they even coming to it for?
Finding something — search, ranked by how much it's actually getting used. Deciding whether to trust what they found — how many people query it, who owns it, how fresh it is.
And agreeing on what something even means — a shared glossary, tied directly to the columns that carry each term.
Now, who's actually building these things?

On the open-source side: one project built around events and graphs. Another built around a shared API and schema. An open edition of a commercial catalog. And a project for the catalog layer underneath the table format itself.
On the other side, sold as finished products: a handful of commercial platforms, named here only — nothing claimed about any of them beyond what each one's own page actually says.
Here's a distinction that's easy to blur, so let's pull it apart properly.
One kind of catalog answers a narrow, technical question: where does this table's data actually live, and who's allowed to read it?

A completely different kind of catalog answers a human one: what does this column actually mean, who owns it, has anyone signed off on it being trustworthy? Same table. Two genuinely different questions.
One more thing worth catching, and it's a small one, but it matters.

A list describing these tools still calls one particular open-source project merely 'low-activity.' Go check that project's own page, though, and it says something considerably stronger: archived, by its own maintainers, specifically for inactivity.
The page itself is right. It's the label describing it that's gone out of date.
So, pulling all of this together.

A catalog is a graph — points for things, named links between them. Scanning on a schedule always leaves some gap; an event-driven update leaves none. Finding something, trusting it, and agreeing on what it means — those are the three jobs people actually come to it for, every day.

Open-source options exist, and so do commercial ones. A technical catalog and a business catalog answer entirely different questions. And a label describing any of this can go stale faster than the thing it's describing.
One more scenario, and there's a twist buried in this one.
Say that same shop switches its tables over to event-based updates, but its dashboards are still only getting swept once a night. A dashboard changes on a Wednesday.
Is the catalog's picture of that dashboard actually current by Thursday — or is it still sitting there stale? And why would it go one way or the other?
answer: Still stale. Freshness isn't some single property that applies to the whole catalog all at once — it belongs to each individual feed going into it, separately.
Switching tables over to event-based updates does absolutely nothing for dashboards. Those are still sitting there, waiting on whatever their own next scheduled sweep happens to be.
